svg.text: MPx Boil-Loop Mini: the same loop, portable, with minimal electrics
Same system as v0.1: pumped through thin steel tubes, held at a boil so lime crusts the microplastics, caught while hot, then cooled by the exchanger and
the coil in the finned body. Now bottle-sized: a 60 W heater, one pump straight off USB-C, and no circuit board, battery, valve or sensor.
fill jug · switch on · water comes out cool
Schematic, not to scale. Ø105 × 350 mm, ~1.3 kg, 1.2 L/h. Right half cut away.
Top row heats the water up; bottom row brings it back down. The exchanger in the middle hands the heat from one row to the other.
C · Body as the radiator (top-down section)
keeps core heat off the coil
The hot parts never touch the shell: the boil happens inside an
insulated core. The exchanger has already brought the water down to
~29°C before the shell coil, so the outside sits within ~1.5°C of
room temperature and is safe to carry while running.
Optional: a wet terracotta sleeve (matka-style) over the fins can
pull a few degrees below room temperature by evaporation.
1 · It only works if the water is hard
Boiling doesn't melt or evaporate plastic. It works because dissolved
lime (CaCO₃) comes out of solution and crusts around the particles
removal after boiling vs water hardness (as CaCO₃) [1]
2 · Energy: the tubes do the work
At 1.2 L/h, heating 25→100°C from cold would take ~121 W. The
exchanger recovers ~95%, so the heater only covers the last few
degrees, steam and losses: ~22 W (16–30 W over 0.8–1.6 L/h). A 60 W
heater on a 65 W USB-C charger has headroom; a 90 Wh power bank gives
Water leaves the exchanger at ~29°C and the body coil trims it to
~27°C in a 25°C room (~37°C on a 35°C day). No waiting: it is
drinkable as it comes out. It can't go below room temperature.
From the tube model (boiltube_sim.py), not measurements.
This decides whether the concept works. Below ~80 mg/L removal falls to ~25–35% [1]. A calcium-dosing cartridge might
help soft water, but that's untested.
The same lime that traps the plastic also coats the tube walls. Use smooth 316 stainless, keep the flow moving and add a
citric-acid descale cycle that runs on its own.
Don't boil in the thin tube.
Boiling in a 3 mm tube makes steam pockets that push water out in bursts. Heat to ~98°C there, and do the actual boil in
the wider dwell coil, which has a vent.
Dwell time is a test variable.
The study boiled for minutes, not seconds. Run 2, 4 and 6 min (change the flow rate or coil length) and count what's
Hot water pulls more out of plastic.
All wetted parts should be steel, glass or ceramic with metal compression fittings. Keep gaskets to a minimum and the
Bringing water to a rolling boil inactivates pathogens [2]. Germs were the top worry in your quiz (34/47), so this is a
selling point the filter-only concepts lack.
USB-C PD trigger (20 V), fuse, rocker, pump, 60 W heater, 130 °C thermostat, 152 °C fuse. No PCB, battery, valve or
sensor: the wax gate and the overflow standpipe do the control.
Two dry-boil cut-offs on the heater block, 20 V only, and the boil coil is vented, so nothing runs under pressure. First
water comes ~15 min after switch-on; until then it overflows back to the jug.

[1] Yu, Z., Wang, J.-J., Liu, L.-Y., Li, Z. & Zeng, E. Y. (2024). Drinking boiled tap water reduces human intake of nanoplastics and microplastics. Environmental Science & Technology Letters 11(3), 273–279. Removal: ~25% in soft water, 34% at 80, 84% at 180, 90% at 300
mg/L CaCO₃. Filtered with a stainless steel mesh.
[2] World Health Organization (2015). Boil water. Technical brief WHO/FWC/WSH/15.02: a rolling boil is enough to inactivate waterborne pathogens.
[3] Rermborirak et al. (2025). FLOro, a low-cost portable microplastic detection system (J. Hazard. Mater. Adv. 19, 100787). The source for the 11 µm filter paper pad.
